question: A patient's hepatitis B serology shows: HBsAg positive, HBeAg positive, anti-HBs negative, anti-HBc IgM positive, HBV DNA 2 × 10⁸ IU/mL. What is the correct interpretation?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Resolved infection is characterised by HBsAg negative, anti-HBs positive, and anti-HBc positive. This patient is HBsAg positive — indicating active infection, not resolution.

answers.text: Acute HBV infection in the immune-tolerant phase

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. HBsAg positive + HBeAg positive + anti-HBc IgM positive + very high HBV DNA (>10⁷ IU/mL) with normal or mildly elevated ALT defines the immune-tolerant phase of acute or early chronic HBV. Anti-HBc IgM confirms recent/acute infection; IgG anti-HBc would suggest chronic infection.
Partially correct pattern, but anti-HBc IgM positivity distinguishes acute from chronic infection. In established chronic HBV, anti-HBc is predominantly IgG, not IgM.
Incorrect. Successful HBV vaccination produces isolated anti-HBs (≥10 mIU/mL) with all other markers negative. This patient is HBsAg positive — vaccination does not produce HBsAg positivity.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the HBV serology roadmap: HBsAg = active infection; anti-HBs = immunity (vaccination or recovery); anti-HBc IgM = acute/recent; IgG = past/chronic; HBeAg + high HBV DNA = active viral replication.

Correct. Anti-HBc IgM is the marker that distinguishes acute from chronic HBV. Its presence alongside HBsAg, HBeAg, and very high viral load indicates acute/early infection in the immune-tolerant phase.
